mercy_translation.text:
And to mention one thing that is itself a very remarkable sign of the Savior's divinity: what mere human being, magician, tyrant, or king ever had such power by himself as to set himself against all idolatry, every army of demons, every form of magic, and all the wisdom of the Greeks—things so powerful, still flourishing, and astonishing everyone—and withstand them all at once, as our Lord, the true Word of God, has done?

Invisible yet exposing the error of each, he alone carries off people from them all: those who formerly worshiped idols now trample them down; those admired for magical practices burn their books; and the wise prefer the interpretation of the Gospels to all other teaching.

They abandon those whom they formerly worshiped, while Christ, whom they mocked as crucified, they now worship, confessing him as God. Those called gods among them are driven away by the sign of the cross, while the crucified Savior is proclaimed throughout the whole inhabited world as God and Son of God. The gods worshiped among the Greeks are denounced by them as shameful, while those who receive the teaching of Christ live more self-controlled lives than they did.

If these and things like them are merely human, let anyone who wishes show comparable deeds from earlier human beings and persuade us. But if these are shown to be and truly are works not of human beings but of God, why do unbelievers act so impiously by refusing to acknowledge the Master who accomplished them?

They suffer something like a person who, from the works of creation, fails to recognize God their Creator. For if from his power throughout the universe they had recognized his divinity, they would also have known that the works of Christ done through the body are not merely human but belong to the Savior of all, the Word of God. Had they known this, as Paul said, “they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.”

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius' examples reflect the apologetic environment of late antiquity and should be historically contextualized.
The final Pauline citation is translated from the Greek wording used in the chapter.
